title: Find the Integer Added to Array II
statement:
You get two integer arrays, `nums1` and `nums2`, and `nums2` is exactly two elements shorter than `nums1`. Delete the elements at two different positions of `nums1`, then add one integer `x` (it may be zero or negative) to every element that is left. Call `x` valid when the outcome holds the same values as `nums2`, each value the same number of times; order does not matter.

Return the smallest valid `x`. The inputs guarantee that at least one valid `x` exists.
constraints: At least one x makes nums1 match nums2 this way
notes:
## Intuition

Adding `x` moves every kept value by the same amount, so after sorting, the smallest kept value of `nums1` must land on the smallest value of `nums2`. Only two values are deleted, so the smallest kept value is one of the three smallest values of `nums1`: there are just three candidates for `x`. Checking a candidate is a subsequence test on the sorted arrays. Trying every pair of deletions instead costs O(n²) pairs, each with a sort.

## Approach

1. Sort `nums1` and `nums2`.
2. For `first = 2`, then `first = 1`, set `x = nums2[0] - nums1[first]`. A larger kept minimum gives a smaller `x`, so the first candidate that works is the smallest.
3. Walk `nums1` in order with a pointer `matched` into `nums2`: when `nums1[i] + x` equals `nums2[matched]`, advance it. If all of `nums2` gets matched, exactly two values were skipped, so return `x`.
4. If neither worked, the guarantee says keeping `nums1[0]` works: return `nums2[0] - nums1[0]`.

## Example 1, step by step

Sorted, `nums1 = [4, 8, 12, 16, 20]` and `nums2 = [10, 14, 18]`. With `first = 2`, `x = 10 - 12 = -2`, and the shifted values are `2, 6, 10, 14, 18`. Scanning them, 10, 14 and 18 match `nums2` in order, so `matched` reaches 3 and the answer is `-2` (4 and 20 are the deleted values).

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) for the sorts; each of the at most two checks is O(n).
- Space: O(1) besides the sorting.

## Pitfalls

- Pairing the two minimums blindly (`nums2[0] - nums1[0]`) fails when the smallest values of `nums1` are the deleted ones, as in `[0, 0, 5, 6, 7]` and `[15, 16, 17]`.
- `x` may be negative, so do not use `-1` or `0` as a "not found" marker.
- The matching pointer only works on sorted arrays; on the original order it misses matches.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `first` | index in sorted `nums1` of the value assumed to be the smallest kept one |
| `x` | the candidate shift that maps `nums1[first]` to `nums2[0]` |
| `matched` | how many values of sorted `nums2` have been matched |
| `i` | position in sorted `nums1` |

narration.2: Sort nums1 so its smallest values come first.
narration.3: Sort nums2 too: its smallest value must come from the smallest kept value of nums1.
narration.4: Only two values are deleted, so the smallest kept one is nums1[2], nums1[1] or nums1[0]; try the one giving the smallest x first.
narration.5: The shift that turns that kept value into the smallest value of nums2.
narration.6: Count how many values of nums2 are matched so far.
narration.7: Scan nums1 in sorted order until all of nums2 is matched.
narration.8: Does this shifted value equal the next value nums2 still needs?
narration.9: Yes: match it. A value that does not match is one of the deleted ones.
narration.12: Every value of nums2 was matched, so exactly two values of nums1 were skipped...
narration.13: ...and this x works; no smaller candidate exists, so return it.
narration.16: Neither larger candidate works, so by the guarantee nums1[0] is kept and gives x.
